# Location Resolution and Empty-Collection Query Decision

This record originally grouped the two phenomena together because they both appeared in the closing checklist for the Atlas 2.4 compatibility window. relative Location resolution requires reviewing the address after request processing; empty collection query syntax requires finding the actual parameter form written by the caller. The initial draft did not turn them into a single unified rule and only recorded the decision to "review them separately." After review, that decision remains, but the scope of the judgment needs to be stated more precisely.

The issue is not that the two names appear on the same page. It is that without an operational boundary for "separately," reading the code can still easily lead from adjacent request logic to a unified normalization step. That may seem convenient, but it mistakes proximity in the code for a relationship between the interfaces. This kind of premature consolidation should be avoided especially during the compatibility window: a counterexample that has been observed cannot be used to explain another user path that has not yet been triggered.

The current investigation entry point is still `lib/httparty/request.rb`. The old investigation record found this file by issue name and call name. It is suitable for focusing on the area near the request object, including Location-related handling, the observation point for the final URI, and the form of the parameters before and after they enter the request. This entry point is retained to make it easier to locate the local position through which the sample passes; it does not mean that the two topics share an implementation, nor does it replace confirmation of caller behavior.

## Directions Compared in the Initial Draft

What was on the table at the time was not a complete request-layer refactor, but two narrower handling directions.

The first direction was to place both relative addresses and collection parameters into a single unified pre-normalization step. Its advantage was that readers would only need to focus on one location, and subsequent calls might also receive more consistent input. The problem is that "consistent" has no clear meaning here. relative Location resolution concerns whether an address still produces the same result after one processing pass and a second processing pass; empty collection query syntax concerns how an empty collection is actually expressed at the call entry point. The former deals with the number of processing passes, while the latter deals with the form of the call. Putting them into the same pre-processing logic does not automatically produce a shared compatibility semantic.

The second direction was to retain two independent lines of observation. The Location line records only the input and output before and after address processing, then compares the result when the same input passes through the relevant processing again; the empty-collection line only looks for forms in existing tests or examples that can trigger the behavior, confirming the request entry point actually used by the user. The initial draft chose the second direction and explicitly did not invent a standard encoding for the empty collection when the available material was insufficient.

This choice does not mean that the two lines can never share underlying code. It only specifies that, during the compatibility window, their proximity to the request layer is not a reason to treat a sample from one topic as evidence for the other. If it is later discovered that both are indeed caused by the same conversion point, their respective inputs, outputs, and trigger paths should still be retained first, followed by discussion of whether the correction points should be combined.

## Review Boundary for relative Location

ATX-206 gives this section a more specific boundary than the initial draft had. The card originally recorded an anomaly in a particular usage of a relative Location, and a counterexample was added afterward. The importance of the counterexample is not that it provides a general rule that can be extrapolated, but that it disproves the convenient assumption that looking only at the first processing pass is sufficient.

The card's subsequent correction states that, in addition to the previously mentioned anomaly in the particular usage, one more case of relative Location resolution remains unconfirmed; its input and output are retained in the consumer compatibility matrix. This should be understood at the original level of granularity. What has been observed is one particular usage, while what remains unconfirmed is another resolution case; the material does not record the two as equivalent or state that they belong to the same failure cause.

Therefore, the decision for the Location line is narrowed to three actions: retain the result after a given input first enters the relevant processing; run the same input through the same processing again and observe whether the result is stable; when a difference appears, retain that set of inputs and outputs in the consumer compatibility matrix rather than extracting only the statement "relative address anomaly."

The third action fills the gap in the initial draft. The old wording treated "processing again" as a small issue to be added later, which made it easy to interpret as an implementation detail. It is now part of the judgment boundary: an apparently reasonable result from the first processing pass does not mean that the second pass will produce the same result. Conversely, even if a counterexample changes on the second pass, that does not allow all relative Locations to be classified as anomalous. The current record does not support such a broad conclusion.

This does not specify what kind of address a relative address should be replaced with, nor does it define any particular output as the only permitted result. The compatibility window needs samples that can distinguish stable behavior from unstable behavior, rather than an abstract rule written first and samples forced to conform to it afterward. The genuinely comparable objects in the current record are the "first processing" and "second processing" results; this is closer to the change the caller may encounter than retaining only one address string.

The initial draft considered placing the observation of the final URI and the resolution judgment in the same explanation. That wording is no longer used. The final URI can help review where the request passed through, but it is not a substitute metric for the correctness of relative-address processing. If the two are tied together, readers may misinterpret "seeing one URI" as "resolution confirmed." This record retains it only as a reading clue near the request.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RelativeLocation Review
    RelativeLocation Review --> First Processing
    First Processing --> Second Processing
    Second Processing --> Retain Input and Output
    [*] --> Empty-Collection Entry Investigation
    Empty-Collection Entry Investigation --> Existing Tests or Examples
    Existing Tests or Examples --> Write Back Uncovered Paths
```

The two lines in the diagram are parallel to preserve the observation order decided this time; they do not mean that the lines will converge on the same request conversion. The relative Location samples proceed through first processing, second processing, and retention of inputs and outputs; the empty-collection side starts from existing tests or examples, with uncovered user paths still returning to the investigation subject.

## The Empty-Collection Parameter Investigation Did Not Borrow Location Samples

ATX-223 is a separate workstream. The card requires using existing tests or examples to trigger empty collection query syntax and writing uncovered user paths back to the card. The item was later marked as having completed failure classification; this only means that the phenomenon encountered during the investigation was assigned to a failure category. This record does not preserve the contents of that category, so it cannot be used to say that the final syntax for the empty collection has been determined.

The decision here is more conservative than for Location: first confirm the trigger method, then discuss parameter normalization. An empty collection may look like an ordinary parameter in a test, but that does not mean the caller's form is covered; an example's failure to trigger does not mean that no user path will trigger it. ATX-223 requires uncovered paths to be written back to the card. This remains in place because it puts the unconfirmed content somewhere that can support continued investigation, rather than burying it in a generalized compatibility conclusion.

One shortcut was discussed but not adopted: directly inferring from ordinary cases of existing request parameters that the empty collection should use the same syntax. This shortcut was abandoned not because ordinary cases have no value, but because an empty collection happens to lack content that can be observed. When content is absent, whether the caller produces a parameter, what form it takes, and whether it passes through the same entry point all require a concrete trigger to confirm. Applying intuition from non-empty cases directly would make the investigation appear finished without increasing confidence about the empty collection.

Also not adopted was attaching the counterexample from ATX-206 after ATX-223 as a reproduction record shared by the two issues. The two cards ask different questions: ATX-206 asks for a comparison of the first and second processing passes for relative Location; ATX-223 asks for the actual entry point for the empty collection query. Sharing one set of samples would only obscure this difference, especially when the samples themselves do not trigger both conditions at the same time.

## Current Decision

What is retained at present is not a decision for a "unified request-layer fix," but two independent compatibility judgment lines.

| Topic | Action retained this round | Inference not made from this |
| --- | --- | --- |
| relative Location resolution | Compare the first and second processing passes for the same input, and retain the input and output | Do not extend one specific anomaly to all relative-address behavior |
| empty collection query syntax | Use existing tests or examples to find the actual trigger entry point, and write uncovered user paths back to ATX-223 | Do not derive empty-collection syntax from ordinary parameters or Location samples |

The contents of the table define the boundary of this decision; they are not intended to organize the two issues into one test format. They state what information is sufficient for each line to move forward independently, as well as what information cannot be transferred across topics. When new samples appear, first determine which row they belong to; do not first ask whether they can support a larger story about request normalization.

`lib/httparty/request.rb` still has a purpose outside this table. When reading the code, one can start from the request adjacency in that file, confirm which local position the sample enters, and then return to the result recorded on the card. A Location sample must correspond to first and second processing; an empty-collection sample must correspond to the actual entry point. If a shared local processing step is found during reading, it can only serve as a lead for further investigation; it cannot be used retroactively to declare that the two topics are the same issue.

An earlier misreading is retained here to avoid repeating it later. Someone initially understood "relative" to mean that only the address obtained on the final pass needed to be confirmed, and therefore tended to retain only the final result. After the counterexample was added, that wording was no longer applicable: the number of processing passes itself changes the meaning of the issue. The old note was not deleted because it explains why the two passes for the same input were later recorded side by side; however, it can no longer be treated as the condition for completing the judgment.

The empty-collection side also has one unresolved question. The card requires a trigger in existing tests or examples, and uncovered user paths must be written back. As long as that path remains empty, the document cannot call any particular query form the conclusion for the compatibility window. This empty item does not prevent the current decision from taking effect: the empty collection does not borrow Location samples or reach a conclusion based on intuition from ordinary parameters.

DOC-16 records another set of interface review subjects, including redirect method preservation matrix and logstash formatter integration. It does not supplement the two judgments on this page. The navigation is retained only because these materials all belong to the compatibility window, so both pages may be encountered while reviewing request behavior; the proximity of the subjects does not mean that the matrix can replace the relative Location input/output record, nor that the formatter review result can explain the empty-collection parameter.

ATX-206 and ATX-223 retain direct navigation. The former contains the added counterexamples and the still-unconfirmed resolution cases, while the latter contains the empty-collection entry investigation and uncovered paths. The document preserves the reasoning behind this decision; the cards continue to hold subsequently discovered samples and investigation traces. In this round, relative Location resolution and empty collection query syntax are handled with different input boundaries and validation methods. Unless a later record provides a concrete processing relationship shared by both lines, the rules will not be merged, counterexamples will not be shared, and completion of one line will not be used to declare the other complete.

# Redirect Method and Formatting Proposal

logstash formatter integration follows a different track. # Forced multipart and JSON Media Decisions

Old links still lead to the short note from June. It placed forced multipart hashes and structured JSON media types under the request-body compatibility record for the Atlas 2.4 compatibility window, making them read like two examples of a single issue. That impression partly reflects the arrangement at the time: clues around the request body were not meant to be scattered across different pages, and grouping the names for retrieval would at least make the same history discoverable.

But in June, "grouping" only addressed where the material was kept, not any conclusion about behavior. The body, request, and hash terms in the old index were reading aids, and `lib/httparty/request.rb` was the first entry point opened. They indicate where the investigation began, not that the two named items changed on the same object, nor that they had to be supported by the same set of regression materials. Declarations or call names near a path are not enough to establish the actual processing relationships for either object.

## The Version Initially Retained

There were three approaches on the table at the time. The first was to describe both items directly as automatic request-body detection. This would take the least space and consolidate search results, but forced multipart hashes concerns when hash-type parameters are classified as multipart, while structured JSON media types concerns the scope of recognition on the media-type side. Describing them as a single determination would erase the difference between the two input conditions.

The second was to split them immediately into two independent decisions. The titles would be clearer, but each page would need its own inputs, observed behavior, and boundaries to investigate. June left no samples sufficient for comparison and no record of whether the fixtures could represent the corresponding inputs. Making both pages look complete at that point would only disguise gaps as established boundaries.

The third was to retain one historical record with the two names side by side, but without shared behavioral assumptions. The path, old search terms, and parallel names would remain; subsequent verification would proceed separately under each name. This was the approach adopted in June. It did not schedule the two checks as a single run, nor did it fix implementation ownership for either named item.

The wording at the time was "do not split them up yet". Later, this could easily be read as "investigate them the same way for now". The original meaning worth preserving is actually narrower: keep the material together for now, but do not combine the evidence. If a sample only shows that hash-type parameters enter multipart, it cannot also establish how structured JSON media types are recognized; the reverse is also true.

## Entry Points and Boundaries

`lib/httparty/request.rb` should remain on this page. The early investigation did start here, and body, request, and hash were the actual reasons the two names were placed together at the time. If only the later reminder not to confuse them were retained while the old entry point was removed, readers would not be able to see why June used side-by-side archiving.

This path serves as local navigation. It takes readers back to the request layer to continue reading, but it does not establish every processing detail for forced multipart hashes, nor can it prove that changes to structured JSON media types necessarily occur in the same place. Similarity between a filename and an issue name is a reason to keep reading, not evidence that establishes an implementation relationship. The local responsibilities associated with the path can help identify the scope of reading, but cannot turn a documentation entry point into a behavior owner.

June also referred loosely to reading the path, reproducing the input, and saving regression results as a single review. Looking back, that wording omitted three distinct actions: reading the request layer can only provide nearby clues; whether a fixture can represent a particular input determines whether an observed behavior can appear independently; where the results are saved affects whether the next investigation can distinguish the two names. They all relate to requests, but they are not the same determination.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Archive
    Archive --> Separate: New sample appears
    Separate --> ForcedHashes: forced multipart hashes
    Separate --> StructuredJSON: structured JSON media types
    ForcedHashes --> Unconfirmed
    StructuredJSON --> Unconfirmed
```

This diagram preserves the sequence of the June arrangement without depicting the two objects as a single processing chain. Side-by-side archiving remains the historical state; only after new samples appear does verification enter separate branches. The unconfirmed items at the ends indicate gaps in the material, not that the same conclusion has already been reached for both objects.

## The Review Recorded in Late September

In late September, ATX-211 first recorded `baseline_recorded`. This singled out forced multipart hashes from the general request-body description, but did not fully establish its boundaries. A subsequent public comment still stated "forced multipart hashes still has one unconfirmed point". So recording a baseline does not mean the issue is closed, nor does it mean June's side-by-side archiving has become a complete rule.

The testing stage was then reassigned to someone who could modify the fixtures. The reason recorded at the time was that this part of the testing stage needed to be handled by someone able to modify the fixtures. What changed was the conditions for verification, not June's file entry point. If the fixtures cannot retain or construct the required inputs, even a clearly identified reading path cannot yield separate determinations from a single reproduction; the ability to adjust fixtures does not, in itself, establish implementation ownership either.

After the review, the results should be viewed at two separate levels. At the documentation level, forced multipart hashes and structured JSON media types remain adjacent names within the same history of the Atlas 2.4 compatibility window, and this page continues to retain them. At the checking level, each item requires inputs that demonstrate its own observed behavior; the other item's results cannot replace its own supporting material.

This page also cannot explain the unconfirmed item in ATX-211 on its behalf. The existing record does not say whether the gap concerns parameter normalization, media-type recognition, or some other neighboring condition. Inferring a specific cause from the word hashes would go one step beyond the material available at the time; saying that the baseline already covers that gap would misread the original addendum.

## Additions That Were Not Adopted

Adding a compatibility matrix for hash and JSON media types was considered. A table would make each of the two names appear to have a row of established combinations, but the existing material does not say whether blank cells mean untested, irrelevant, or confirmed unaffected. Drawing those blank cells would imply a stronger judgment than June's provisional grouping, so the matrix was not added.

Using "request encoding" as a unified archive name was also considered. The name would work well for searches, but it would compress the forced nature of multipart and the recognition of structured JSON media types into one broad label. It would be more convenient for the old directory, but would remove distinctions that the decision record needs to preserve.

Another proposed addition was to rewrite the old page as two rules that would look tidier now. This could reduce June's ambiguous wording, but would erase the fact of why the material was gathered under the same entry point at the time. Old references still lead to this page, and the historical classification itself is worth preserving, so the later approach of separate verification was not used to overwrite the earlier text.

## Original Wording Still Retained

This does not mean June's classification is still sufficiently accurate. What is outdated is the optimistic reading that "if we put them together, the distinction will naturally become clear later". What remains usable is the narrower arrangement: retain the historical entry point and place the two names side by side without treating either as evidence for the other; when new behavior appears, first use `lib/httparty/request.rb` to review the objects actually traversed, then save samples and fixture issues under their respective names.

structured JSON media types was included in this history in June because compatibility issues around the request body needed to be reviewed together at the time. This old record does not list the various media-type forms or specify what changes would occur for each. If a specific report arrives later, the changed syntactic unit and an actual request sample should be retained; merely adding a broader umbrella term here will not make the boundaries clearer.

The follow-up records for forced multipart hashes have already shown that separate checking remains valuable, but at least one point is still unconfirmed. This page preserves the grouping of the material, the rejected combined descriptions, and the direction of separate verification after the review. It does not treat a shared entry point as a shared conclusion, nor does it fill in unconfirmed parts as settled decisions.

# MIME Priority and Compression Negotiation Plan

This time, the original entry record has been condensed into a locally testable proposal, but search hits have not been written up as established behavior. The scope remains within `lib/httparty/request.rb`: the current index confirms that this is an existing rb module, which can be used for code reading and checking historical behavior; specific ownership should be determined by the reference relationship between `internal/ATLAS` and its `v_prev`. The anomaly records adjacent to 303 body cleanup / request marshal state remain in DOC-22 and are not merged into this proposal.

### Disagreements left open for now

The multipart dispute is not "whether to send multipart," but which input determines MIME when multiple inputs appear at the same time. Three paths can be tried:

- Explicit `content_type` takes precedence over the assembly result. The caller's intent is relatively stable, but the cost is that when `body` already contains `parts` or a file, the declaration and the actual shape may be inconsistent.
- The assembly result of `parts`, file input, or `stream` takes precedence. The request shape is easier to align with MIME, but this will change the expectations of callers that have already supplied an explicit type.
- Use a separate branch for forced multipart hashes instead of applying the same decision as for ordinary `parts`. The compatibility boundary will be clearer, and the conditions will be easier to split from the main path, but future maintenance costs will be higher.

These three are still candidates, not priorities that have been finalized. First, use request.rb to trace `body`, `mime`, `parts`, `content_type`, `method`, and `name` to identify the actual local adjacency, then decide which conditions can be tested together. `stream`, `used`, `type.`, and `type` are currently retained only as lookup points; runtime semantics should not be inferred from them.

### How to try the compression side

Record compression negotiation with headers separately. There are two candidate approaches: first, retain the negotiation headers already provided by the caller and only observe whether anything needs to be added during request construction; second, normalize the relevant headers before negotiation so that the constructed request carries only the normalized values. The former is more conservative toward existing callers, but may leave mutually inconsistent declarations; the latter makes it easier to obtain a consistent request shape, but may silently alter information originally provided by the caller.

This part should not share a single "looks successful" criterion with the selection of MIME. Each sample must record at least whether the input is an ordinary body, `parts`, a file, a hash, or `stream`, whether `content_type` was supplied explicitly, the original request header values, and the result visible after the call returns. A successful sample can only show that this input path worked; a failed sample alone cannot show whether it was caused by MIME precedence or header negotiation.

### Minimal shape of the experiment log

Prepare two comparison groups first, without trying to list every permutation at once:

1. With `parts` or file input, use an explicit `content_type` in one case and no explicit type in the other, and observe whether the final MIME changes with the input shape.
2. For the same request shape, retain one set of compression-related headers, then remove or modify one of the values, recording the success and failure results separately.
3. Keep forced multipart hashes as a separate sample; do not merge its result into ordinary `parts` samples.
4. If `stream` follows a different construction path, record it on a separate line instead of replacing it with the conclusion for an ordinary body.

The quality side should directly retain these quality samples; every sample must include the version, environment, and CI job, and failed nodes must be traceable back to the corresponding input. The implementation side should confirm only the declarations, call adjacency, and actual diff for request.rb. The integration side should provide caller screenshots or old links to help reproduce the entry point, but should not use screenshots to determine the ownership of MIME. This way, each participant adds only evidence within their own boundary, rather than treating an old link as proof of behavior.

### When to withdraw

If the review still cannot identify who makes the choice between `body` and `mime`, or if the changes in compression negotiation with headers cannot be correlated with the returned result, stop expanding the candidate approaches and leave the items unresolved. What is being withdrawn is the experimental path newly added this time; untested candidates should not be written as compatibility commitments, and the existing path should not be deemed incorrect based on a single failed sample.

The priority between explicit `content_type` and the multipart assembly result has not yet been decided, nor has it been decided whether compression negotiation may normalize the caller's headers. Once the samples and local references line up, proceed to the formal change.

# 303 Cleanup and Request Marshalling Troubleshooting Tree

This page starts with an investigation that is very easy to conflate: the caller sees unexpected body handling after 303, while someone else sees state changes when reusing a request. Both can be found under the same terms in old records, ultimately point to `lib/httparty/request.rb`, and were therefore placed on the same track in early records. In the current investigation, first separate response redirects from request object reuse; only when the evidence from both sides lines up should they be put back into the same reproduction.

## Conclusions Left by the Old Records

The early note contained only one useful but incomplete statement: when you see 303, check body cleanup first; if reprocessing remains unstable, inspect request marshal state. It works as an entry point, not as attribution. The old note did not distinguish among whether the body was present, whether the request had already been rebuilt, and whether the same object was passed through the processing path again. As a result, it did not preserve reproductions that changed only one condition at a time.

Do not delete this old conclusion. It explains why the old investigation started with `redirect` and `body`, and why it later reached `raw`. However, when executing the tree below, the old conclusion can only determine where to look first; it cannot directly determine what to fix.

## First Collect Reproducible Evidence

Before starting, pin down the following in the same record:

- The trigger method: whether it is the `get` entry point or request options passed through `options`;
- Whether the URI before the redirect, method, headers, and body are empty, as well as the URI after the redirect;
- The fields and values of the request object during the first processing pass; do not construct another "equivalent" object before the second pass;
- The `raw` contents seen by each processing pass, and whether the output is response content, diagnostic text, or a regenerated request;
- The library version, runtime environment, and test task used. Quality review must retain at least the version, environment, CI job, failed node, and actual command executed; when there is only one failure summary, do not treat it as a stable behavior record.

If the body or raw content has already been lost from the evidence, mark it as missing first; do not fill it in with a truncated log fragment. For this issue, an empty body, an unrecorded body, and a body that was cleaned up are not the same thing.

## Decision Tree

```text
An anomaly is observed
├─ Appears only after 303
│  ├─ The second request has a body → Check request rebuilding and body cleanup after the redirect
│  ├─ The second request has no body → Preserve both response and request records, then check whether this is the expected path
│  └─ The second request cannot be confirmed → Stop at the response boundary and add the original record
├─ The first pass is normal, but the next pass changes
│  ├─ The request object has changed → Check the state difference before and after marshal
│  ├─ The object has not changed but the output has → Check the processing entry point and output construction order
│  └─ There are no two outputs → The symptom cannot be attributed to request marshal state
└─ Both types of symptom appear together
   ├─ 303 can first be reproduced independently → Follow the first branch
   ├─ Repeated processing can then be reproduced independently → Follow the second branch
   └─ It can only be reproduced in combination → Do not submit a cleanup or rebuild action
```

The tree's "has a body" refers only to the content actually carried by the second request; it does not refer to a body text segment still retained in the response log. Record these two locations in separate columns during the check, so that the judgment is not merged just because they use the same field name.

## 303 Branch: Confirm the Boundary First

The condition for entering this branch is that the anomaly appears after 303 and that records from before and after the redirect are available. First compare four things: the status code, the target URI, the request method, and the body. If you can see only the status code and target URI, you still cannot confirm whether body cleanup occurred; if you can see only empty output, you also cannot confirm that the request body was removed.

In `lib/httparty/request.rb`, start tracing back from the local declarations related to `redirect`, then follow the direct adjacencies of `body`, `get`, `options`, and `raw` to inspect the processing order. Here, verify only against the file contents of `v_prev`; do not infer the complete call chain from filenames. If the same request is rewrapped after the redirect, record the objects before and after wrapping separately; do not write "rebuild" as "cleanup." The former changes the object being inspected, while the latter describes a content-processing action.

If the method, URI, and body after the redirect can all be confirmed in the same output, run another comparison that changes only the target URI. Keep the original headers in the comparison as well; otherwise, changes to the headers will make the body difference impossible to explain. If the comparison cannot complete, stop at "symptom confirmed, cause unconfirmed"; do not submit temporary body-deletion logic.

## request marshal state Branch

The condition for entering this branch is that the same request has at least two results: one from the first processing pass and one from the next. Place an object snapshot between the two processing actions; do not compare only the final outputs. Check the following separately:

1. Before the first processing pass, is the input still held by the caller?
2. After the first processing pass, were the method, URI, headers, body, or options changed?
3. Was the content generated after marshal put back into the original request?
4. Did the second processing pass use the original object, a copied object, or an already wrapped object?

If the object has already changed before the second processing pass, record the changed fields first, then determine whether this is a designed state transition or unintended residue. Do not use "the second result is different" as a direct substitute for field differences. If the object snapshots are identical but the outputs differ, check whether both passes went through the same `get` / `options` entry point and whether there was different raw input; if the entry points or inputs differ, split them into two records first.

The recovery action for repeated processing may act only on objects created by this reproduction. Do not write back to the body held by the caller just to stabilize the second output, and do not marshal the request multiple times without snapshots. Doing so changes both the input and the number of processing passes, making it impossible to determine which step caused the change.

## How to Stop When the Two Branches Intersect

When the 303 branch and the marshal branch are both valid, first collect the minimum evidence: one standalone 303 redirect and one repeated-processing case without a redirect. Use the same input form for both, but do not assume that they share the same request instance. The first set should answer only what the body and method are after the redirect; the second should answer only whether the object changes during the next processing pass.

If the standalone 303 reproduction is normal but the combined scenario is anomalous, prioritize preserving the complete order of the combined scenario: who constructs the request first, when the response is processed, when the body is read, and when marshal runs again. Do not expand the standalone reproduction result into a conclusion about the combined scenario. If repeated processing is already anomalous on its own, do not investigate redirect yet; otherwise, the two variables will mask each other in the same output.

Stop modifying and only add records in any of the following cases: there are no paired before-and-after URI records; there are no two request snapshots; the body appears only in truncated logs; the version or environment is not recorded; or the reproduction depends on options that the caller did not retain. Stopping does not mean judging the issue invalid; it preserves the smallest boundary that can currently be confirmed.

## Several Easily Misread Points in the Evidence

"Body is empty" has at least three forms: the body of the request object is empty, the content sent to `net::http` is empty, or the body was not printed in the log. Record them separately. `raw` cannot replace these three records either; raw can help confirm the content actually generated, but it cannot show when the object changed.

"Processing again" also has two meanings: sending the same request through the processing entry point again, or creating a new request from the result of the first processing pass. The record must state which one occurred. The latter is not a stable reproduction of the former, even if URI, method, and headers look the same.

When `options` contains body-related settings, preserve the shape of the structure passed in; do not copy out only a final string. For the `get` entry point, record the options actually passed by the caller; for a directly constructed request, record the object after construction. The record formats for the two entry types may differ, but results missing entry-point information cannot be classified as the same type.

## Code Entry Points and Adjacent Materials

The current code verification entry points remain:

- Repository: `internal/ATLAS`
- revision: `v_prev`
- File: `lib/httparty/request.rb`
- Search first for: `redirect`, `body`, `get`, `options`, `raw`, `net::http`

This set of terms is used only to locate the local declarations and adjacency relationships that this page actually concerns. After finding the names in `request.rb`, continue recording directly visible calls or data transfers; do not write relationships not seen in that revision as a definite chain. The old investigation entry point is retained here because the issue name and call name still lead readers to this record, not because the path itself has proven ownership.

If the reproduction subsequently enters multipart bytes with mixed encoding, switch to DOC-23; that section records a separate migration track. Do not put the result of the encoding conversion back into this page's 303 or request marshal state conclusion; this page retains it only as the boundary for an adjacent investigation.

## On-Call Addendum

When a new sample arrives, first write one of "303," "repeated processing," or "both intersect" under the title, then attach the shortest request/response pair. Do not attach only the failed assertion. Quality review must be able to see the version, environment, and CI job; interface review must be able to see the actual caller result. If either type of material is missing, retain the unconfirmed status.

Confirming that the body was cleaned up after the redirect establishes only the body cleanup symptom for that sample; confirming that the object fields changed across two marshal passes establishes only the request marshal state change for that sample. Only after both records are complete may they be written into the same fix discussion. The old conclusion left earlier should continue to be retained as an entry point and must not override the new branching result.

Before: issue name / call name

The section below preserves the original migration method so it can be recognized when recovering old notes; it is no longer the review sequence.

- Use an issue name or call name to reach the file, then search the same page for `body`, `encoding`, `bytes`, `utf`, `field`.
- Treat the first hit location as the destination after migration; when several multipart fragments are nearby, choose one based on the impression formed while reading at the time.
- If the caller's description does not match the terms in the file, return to the original issue name and search again, keeping both descriptions side by side.

The value of this method is that it preserved the old entry points; its drawback is also clear: a keyword hit does not automatically connect to a specific caller. If an old page says "the field is already handled uniformly here", read that as a working judgment made at the time, not as a substitute for the later review.

ATX-214 changed the entry point to the discovery workflow for "mixed-encoding multipart bytes", starting from the repository root, and required keeping the final list of hits. This change did not remove the old keywords, but returned them to a navigational role: they help locate potentially relevant places, while the final list shows which objects this search actually reached.

When following the procedure, first note the full phrase, then save the final list of hits from this search. Only then inspect the locations in `lib/httparty/request.rb` that connect to that list. Local declarations, parameter names or adjacent text in the file may be recorded, but do not extend them into proof that the caller has already passed in a particular, definite byte representation.

A caller walkthrough was added to the review. It should be kept with the list of hits, rather than tucked back into the old keyword notes: the former answers which call relationships were followed this time, while the latter preserves only why this location was originally found. - **Search entry point**: the full issue phrase, along with any issue names or call names that still need to be retained.
- **File locations**: paths in the list of hits; `lib/httparty/request.rb` may appear here, but should not stand apart from the list as the sole basis for a conclusion.

# Base URI host isolation decision record

During the compatibility window, base URI host isolation needs its own record rather than being folded into generic URI issues. The old investigation notes can point readers to `lib/httparty/request.rb`, but they aren't enough to establish which input determines the request's target host.

The provisional approach is to distinguish the request inputs first: a relative URI and a URI that already includes a host cannot share a single explanation of "use base URI." The former provides no host in the input; the latter already has a source for the host. Even if both end up with the same target, that doesn't make them the same processing path.

Two formulations were rejected at the time. One attributed the host entirely to base URI; the other treated finding `request.rb` as a conclusion about behavior. The former left out the input differences, and the latter left out the call site. Follow-up samples need to capture base URI, the URI form, and the request target together before deciding how broadly the old explanation can still be retained.

# Base URI Host Isolation Decision Record

base URI host isolation was included in the compatibility window not because of a single failed request, but because "host" in the old records was often treated as a term whose meaning had already been fully explained. Some people saw that base URI was set and understood the request target to always come from there; others saw an input that itself included a host and recorded the target change as a failure of base URI isolation. Both descriptions captured part of what happened, but collapsed the host source, request input, and final target into a single judgment.

The first draft already designated `lib/httparty/request.rb` as the starting point for reading. That starting point remains after review: the old investigation records led into this file from the issue name and call name, and this is indeed where reading should begin when examining declarations and adjacent references near request construction. A separate misunderstanding needs to be corrected: a path can help locate what should be examined, but cannot by itself serve as evidence of the caller's input. A filename will not tell readers whether a wrapper handled URI earlier, nor will it automatically reveal the final request target.

This decision addresses only the relationship between base URI, request input URI, and the target host. Path joining, ports, protocols, authentication headers, and redirects may all appear during the same reading, but they must not be mixed into conclusions about host isolation simply because they also involve URI or target changes. They have their own input conditions; collectively calling them "exceptions to the host rules" here would instead make it impossible to tell from the regression records what is actually being compared.

## Decision Made

Within the compatibility window, base URI host isolation is recorded as a separate request compatibility item. Every sample available for review should state three things together: what base URI is, whether the request input is a relative URI or a URI that already includes a host, and what the actual request target is. If any one of these is missing, the record may be retained as a lead, but cannot support a judgment of "isolation succeeded" or "isolation failed."

The decision establishes the order of evaluation, not a predetermined policy of overriding, retaining, or rejecting anything. First confirm whether the request input already provides a host; then examine whether base URI is the context for that input or another source to be compared; only then describe the request target. Previous shorthand such as "base URI determines the host" will no longer be used as a compatibility conclusion. It may remain as a working hypothesis from the old investigation, because it explains why request construction was examined at the time; however, subsequent samples can no longer be classified on the basis of that statement.

This also means that the result string alone is not enough. Two samples yielding the same host do not automatically show that they underwent the same processing; two samples yielding different hosts do not automatically show that isolation failed either. Evaluation must return to where the host entered the request: whether the relative input did not provide a host, or a full URI already brought the host in. Only when this source is clearly recorded do the results become meaningfully comparable.

The items to record are ordered as follows. The states in the diagram are only items that need to be retained during review; they do not indicate that the implementation has fixed state transitions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> base_uri
  state "base URI" as base_uri
  state "Relative URI input" as relative_uri
  state "URI input with a host" as absolute_uri
  state "Request target" as request_target
  base_uri --> relative_uri
  base_uri --> absolute_uri
  relative_uri --> request_target
  absolute_uri --> request_target
```

## Approaches Compared During Review

The first candidate was to continue using the old informal judgment, treating host as an incidental property of base URI. It has one clear advantage: for calls that pass only relative paths, the description is short, and readers can quickly find where base URI is set. The problem is that this shorthand does not explain whether the request input itself already has a host. Once samples using a full URI are included, readers cannot tell whether that host came from the input, the context, or earlier processing at the call site. Erasing this prerequisite just to keep a sentence tidy would cause subsequent differences in results to be misrecorded as random regressions.

The second candidate was to extract only the local declarations from `lib/httparty/request.rb` and then identify that file as responsible for host behavior. This goes a step beyond looking only at the issue title: the area around the request object is indeed an appropriate place to check inputs and reference relationships. However, what kind of URI the caller passes, whether it handles base URI earlier inside a wrapper, and where the final request is sent are still facts along the call chain. If the file location is presented as the complete answer, readers will think that verification of the caller has been completed, when in fact only the relevant location has been found.

The third candidate was more radical: group samples only by the final target host and stop recording the input form. This method is suitable for quickly summarizing observable behavior, but not for compatibility judgments. It would place "the target obtained from a relative URI in a particular context" and "the target whose host is already included in a full URI" side by side as records of the same type. The table would appear to contain more information, but the host source would be lost. This grouping method was not adopted after review.

The approach ultimately retained is slower but can be revisited: the host source comes before the resulting host. It does not require a generalized matrix for every caller, nor does it require deriving rules for all requests from a single local sample; it requires that, when a judgment is needed, the two types of URI input not be conflated into the same example.

## Differences to Preserve in Comparisons

A relative URI is the first input type. It does not specify a host in the input itself, so it is easy to focus only on base URI when reading. For this type of sample, the record must explicitly say "relative URI," rather than retain only a path fragment. The subsequent review focuses on how this input is received near request construction and where the final request target ends up. Without these conditions, no definitive judgment about the host can be made solely because base URI is set.

The second type is a URI that already includes a host. This is the counterexample most easily missed by the old interpretation, because it forces the person recording it to distinguish information already present in the input from the result of subsequent processing. Some brief records in the past would say "host changed" or "host did not change," without explaining whether the request already carried a host at the start. Such results cannot explain the source of the change, nor can they be compared side by side with samples using a relative URI. The current approach requires retaining the condition that a full URI was used; when the processing has not yet been confirmed, it is preferable to mark it as pending review rather than apply conclusions for a relative URI to it.

The third type can be used to check old assumptions: results from the same call site under different base URI settings. Its value is in helping identify whether context changes have been mistaken for stable semantics, not in letting a single call site support conclusions for all users. If this comparison produces different targets, first look back at whether the input already includes a host; if the input forms differ, the difference should not be assigned to the same branch. Only if the input forms are the same should the relationship between request construction and the call site be investigated further.

These three types of comparison are not a test checklist requiring a fixed execution order. They are distinctions that must not be omitted when recording a judgment. Without these distinctions, "success," "failure," "override," or "inheritance" would all go beyond the available material, and it would later be impossible to know which input to return to for verification.

## Responsibility Boundaries

The public interface team maintains the problem definition: the discussion here concerns the relationship between base URI, request input URI, and the target host. Interface documentation needs to let callers identify whether their input is a relative URI or a URI with a host, rather than merely provide a generic support indicator. If a conclusion depends on a call sample that has not yet been retained, its conditions should remain explicit; the interface name must not substitute for the facts of the sample.

Implementation review begins at `lib/httparty/request.rb`, examining where the request object receives URI and the adjacent references visible there. The review should return the input relationships or call relationships actually observed at that location. If the judgment depends on a caller's earlier wrapper, keep that call site on the list of code to read; do not document speculation as a module responsibility simply because the current file is close to the request object.

Quality review preserves sample conditions that can be consistently identified again. The version, environment, and job to which the execution result belongs must be traceable to one another before that sample can be used to change a compatibility judgment. Screenshots or verbal feedback without these conditions may suggest a problem, but are insufficient to distinguish the results of a relative URI from those of a full URI. The quality team does not define semantics on behalf of the interface team or fill in the call chain on behalf of the implementation team; it confirms whether results under the stated conditions can still be identified and reviewed again.

Caller feedback is used to recover the actual entry point. If feedback claims a dependency on host isolation, it needs to provide at least the form of the URI passed in, where base URI is set, and the observed target. Feedback that only says "it used to work" or "the target changed" can help locate the issue, but cannot be directly elevated to a compatibility conclusion. This boundary also prevents callers' historical impressions from being documented as implementation facts about request construction.

## Review Starting Points and Items to Retain

When reading again, first use `lib/httparty/request.rb` to find the local position where the request object receives URI and its adjacent references, then return to the specific call site to confirm the URI input form. Do not start with "how host should behave" and reason backward to the code; that makes it easy to treat the old interpretation as a premise to be proved. base URI should enter the comparison after the input form has been confirmed, while the final request target should appear at the end of the record as the observed result.

The old investigation records still retain the lead of "entering the request code from the issue name and call name." It is useful when locating base URI-related material again, especially when distinguishing objects near request construction from caller wrappers. Retaining this lead does not mean revising the old text into the current rule: the old text did not preserve enough input conditions and can still serve only as navigation.

What is still missing is a real caller sample that records base URI, the URI input form, and the request target together. Once a sample is found, its results should be added using the distinctions in this decision; if it actually reveals authentication, redirects, or other URI processing, record that separately rather than forcing an adjacent issue back under the host isolation heading.

# Digest qop Compatibility Proposal

This records the narrow issue encountered during the Atlas 2.4 window: when the qop value in a digest challenge is unquoted, should the existing path treat it as the same input as the quoted form? The preliminary investigation started from `lib/httparty/net_digest_auth.rb`; this module was the entry point for reviewing digest behavior at the time.

The provisional hypothesis is that the issue is not in the authentication flow as a whole, but in where the qop text is processed before entering digest calculation. If it is rewritten immediately after reading the challenge, later concatenation may receive a value different from the original challenge; if the original text is retained throughout, the unquoted value may be carried into a location that accepts only the canonical form.

The recommendation is to start with a small experiment without changing the public interface: prepare the same qop input in quoted and unquoted forms, pass each through the existing digest entry point, and capture the request headers and results. There are two candidate changes:

1. Normalize qop to an internal form when reading it;
2. Retain the text from the challenge and process it only before constructing the digest response.

The draft currently leans toward the second option because the change surface is smaller and it is easier to roll back. This judgment is not yet supported by enough counterexamples, especially since the behavior when qop appears together with other challenge fields is still unclear.

Rollback condition: if handling the unquoted form changes the request headers for existing quoted inputs, or requires extending the compatibility branch to authentication paths outside digest, stop this trial. We still need to confirm where the test record should be filed relative to an existing test case.

# Digest qop Compatibility Proposal

This proposal has remained under the Atlas 2.4 compatibility window. It originally aimed to answer just one local question: where to start looking when qop in a digest challenge is unquoted. It was not intended to define digest authentication in full. The earlier investigation pointed both the issue name and the call name to `lib/httparty/net_digest_auth.rb`, so subsequent verification still starts here rather than by changing the caller first.

The initial draft's assessment has been retained: at the time, the preference was to preserve the qop text in the challenge and process it just before constructing the digest response. The reasoning was that rewriting the input first might affect subsequent field concatenation; the other candidate was to normalize qop to an internal form as soon as it was read. Both options assumed that the difference between "unquoted" and "quoted" was limited to local text normalization. Actual samples had not established that assumption at the time.

That assessment had an easily overlooked premise. qop does not arrive as a standalone configuration item; it is part of a digest challenge. Any trial must examine the rest of the challenge fields and the resulting authentication header together. Observing only a normalized qop string cannot establish whether the request still completes along its original path. The initial draft treated "processing later" as the safer choice, but that was only a way to narrow the trial scope, not an interface decision.

The verification added later did not expand the issue into an authentication refactor. ATX-217 provided a reusable entry-point description: run a source snippet that directly triggers "unquoted digest qop" through the existing entry point, and save the input and the tool's actual output. The card also recorded the `toolchain_pinned` action, so this verification can at least pin down the tool used for the run without mixing differences between toolchains into the qop assessment.

Retain three things during verification: the challenge text supplied to the entry point, the generated authentication header, and the tool's actual output. The first confirms that the test really covers unquoted qop; the second allows comparison of whether processing extends beyond the local qop boundary; the third helps distinguish failures in authentication computation, request sending, or the sample itself. There is no requirement here to list every digest field again, but qop must not be recorded separately from the rest of the challenge.

The recommendation is to narrow the trial to two steps. First, leave `lib/httparty/net_digest_auth.rb` unchanged and save a set of raw samples and outputs using the entry point described in ATX-217. If the results show that the quoted and unquoted cases differ only in the textual form of qop, then compare the two candidate processing points. The first normalizes qop immediately after reading the challenge; the second preserves the original text and normalizes it only when generating the values needed for the digest response. Both candidates must rerun the quoted samples; getting only the new samples to pass is not enough.

The old proposal's wording that "processing later is always safer" is no longer used. The available verification material supports treating it only as a candidate, not documenting it as default behavior. Earlier processing may reduce downstream branches; later processing may stay closer to the original challenge text. Which is appropriate depends on the actual authentication headers and outputs, not this page's preference. For that reason, the proposal does not recommend adding a broad compatibility fallback without samples.

The stop conditions remain clearer than the acceptance conditions: if handling unquoted qop changes the authentication headers for existing quoted samples, withdraw that candidate; if it requires touching authentication paths outside the digest challenge, that is also outside this trial's scope; if the output cannot distinguish authentication-header differences from entry-point differences, add samples first rather than combining the assessments. In these cases, retain the inputs, authentication headers, and tool outputs, and do not write unverified attributions back into the interface documentation.

Two points remain unresolved. First, this page has not confirmed where the existing entry point retains the original qop text. Second, whether there are representative samples combining other challenge fields with unquoted qop still needs to be determined from the actual verification material. DOC-27 are related to this page but do not provide the digest conclusions needed here.

This page is still referenced because it preserves the options, entry point, and withdrawal boundaries from that time. Its preference for "processing later" belongs to the old proposal and should not be treated as an authoritative description of present digest behavior. If clear samples become available later, the conclusion should be recorded separately in the relevant interface records, not backfilled as though this proposal had already reached it.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Window Close Checklist

As the window nears its end, use only the current entry point for these checks. The old criteria treated `host boundary` as a sufficient boundary between the borrowed state and the exit action, so this checklist does not track the full release process or fill in assessments for other entry points. Check whether the current entry point is still borrowed, whether the final output is complete, when it is returned, and whether a rollback can return to the original action.

First, open `docs/adj-spec/release/spec-quality-signal-board-pre-window-close-short-checklist.md`. If the entry point no longer points to the version used for this window, stop here. A similarly named page is no substitute for the original entry point; do not clear out the original page or the content left there at the time. If you see old routes or leftover actions, preserve the state as found as well; do not merge them into a new release path in this checklist.

1. [ ] Confirm that the current entry point is still in the borrowed state. If there are no collection or execution records, do not fill in zeros; just record the gap and withhold approval. The old checklist assumed the entry point alone was enough to establish the state and did not check bypass paths separately.
2. [ ] Wait until the final output has stabilized before returning the entry point. If the output is still changing, or you can only see results for some fixtures, keep waiting. Do not return it first and then use later records to retroactively establish that the window has ended.
3. [ ] Look for `reproduction trace`. If you find it, leave it unchanged; it is not a temporary log that can be cleaned up. If you cannot find it, do not write an account of a failure from memory, and do not delete the current entry point because it is missing.
4. [ ] Check against `last URI`. If it has not appeared, stop the window closeout under the old criteria. At the time, this judgment was treated as the only stop signal; do not substitute another value on the spot or use partial output instead.

When a rollback is needed, first save a pre-change route snapshot, then follow adj-spec's original exit action. If the rollback entry point still points to the old exit action, stop the operation and restore the routes from the snapshot; do not wire up a new exit path at the end of the window. No alternative recovery action is documented here.

After the return is complete, check the final output once more. If it differs from the output before the return, record the entry point, the output, and the order of events around the return in one place; do not declare the window complete yet. The handoff section should also include the person handing over, the person taking over, and the confirmation time; if these values are missing, do not treat blanks as a completed handoff.

# Quality Signal Cache Trade-off Decision Record

The debate over the cache and the original execution context left two different positions on record. The earlier view was that separating `request policy` out of `raw request` would make it easier to explain the difference between the failure exits. A later addendum was more conservative: curated cache records cannot replace the original spec-quality-signal replay itself. Both passages remain here, not because they fully agree, but because the later decision grew out of the gaps in the earlier one.

The v1 assessment did not deny the value of `raw request`; its focus at the time was on why the two exits differed. That made `request policy` the main point of comparison. This framing was convenient enough for a single replay. But once someone reconstructed a similar input from material already summarized in the cache, it could no longer establish whether the new sample still followed the original failure path. The old wording, "lean toward splitting," is therefore retained, but no longer represents the adopted trade-off on its own.

The records for month 12 made it impossible to keep treating this as a naming issue. ATXA-006 completed failure classification before moving into handling. The classification gave a direction for inspecting samples, but did not produce a new input that could replace the original replay. The reason recorded when ATXA-010 was blocked was also straightforward: the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields. With the fields still unconfirmed, they should not be filled in using the forms already in the cache, much less used to declare the reconstructed environment equivalent to the original execution context.

There was also a proposal at the time to keep the cache and build a fresh environment, on the grounds that local runs could produce comparable results and a rebuilt environment would be cleaner. That proposal was not adopted. What was rejected was not the cache, but the practice of "replacing the original spec-quality-signal replay with a similar environment": similar inputs would change the conditions around the failure exits, while the upstream fields remained unconfirmed. Keep the cache so people can find old samples; keep the original execution context so they can determine what those samples actually did.

The review of ATXA-015 singled out the public entry point. The original spec-quality-signal must be checked again through the public entry point; local results are only material for locating the issue. This addendum did not report a completed recheck, nor did it promote local results to results from the public entry point. It only clarified the order of assessment: first follow the original sample through the original entry point, then decide which fragments in the cache warrant further investigation.

## Decisions Adopted in This Version

After recovery, take only the first current revision record. Do not include later summaries in this trade-off decision yet, because they may contain curated findings that appeared only after the original replay. This restriction does not mean later records have no value; it means they cannot be used to infer the first record that appeared at recovery.

The original spec-quality-signal replay must be retained. Do not reconstruct a similar input as a substitute. Here, "retain" includes allowing reviewers to start reading from the original entry point. It does not mean deleting the cache, nor does it require creating a new environment from scratch every time.

`request policy` remains comparison material. It can help show which side each of the two failure exits falls on, but cannot by itself prove that the input, entry point, and execution context are identical. The earlier records supporting the split remain useful, but only for this narrower purpose.

Keep the cache records, but use them to locate material and narrow the scope of inspection. Results in the cache do not automatically override `raw request`, nor do they constitute substitute verification of the public entry point. If a first difference appears between the cache and the original replay, preserve that difference on the original path rather than explaining it away with summary results first.

## Still Open

ATXA-019 later added verification by an actual consumer: read from the original entry point through to the current revision, stopping at the first difference. That card has completed interface review and work has started, but it is not recorded here as having produced a result. It adds an inspection direction, not further approval of the trade-off between the cache and the original execution context.

The upstream input fields also remain an outstanding blocker. Once the fields are confirmed, the comparison granularity for `request policy` may need to be reassessed. Until then, do not extend v1's conclusion about splitting. The exit-action material has not changed the decisions above: the cache does not replace the original execution context, and the original execution context is not to be rebuilt on the strength of a single local curation pass.

The related entry points are retained as ATXA-006, ATXA-010, ATXA-015, and ATXA-019. The earlier items explain why a similar input was not reconstructed; the last records that verification by an actual consumer is still in progress. This page still reflects the cache-versus-replay trade-off made at the time. It should not be read as an up-to-date operating procedure that already covers all callers.

# Quality Signal Dashboard User FAQ

This page collects three questions users have asked repeatedly. It covers failing samples produced by specs and fixtures, and how those samples fit into regression tiers and unstable-signal attribution. The Quality Signal Dashboard has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria; citing a sample elsewhere does not automatically turn it into a finding about a shared interface.

**Where are the current entry point and revision?**

The entry point is still `docs/adj-spec/faq/spec-quality-signal-board-three-user-questions.md`. The available materials are labeled as a `latest-known` export, with the body and attachments maintained by adj-spec. The export label only tells you where this copy was obtained; it is not a substitute for the revision actually used by a failing sample. When reporting an issue, first put the spec, fixture, raw results, and the revision from that run in one place. That way, symptoms from an old sample won't be attributed to the current revision.

**When both statuses have appeared, which one should we keep?**

First record both statuses in the order they occurred, then confirm whether they refer to the same object. A later green result cannot erase an earlier failure, nor can the earlier failure alone prove that the current revision still has a problem. ATXA-014 is used for this kind of two-status cross-check. If only zero results remain in a section of the record, the approach in ATXA-005 is to check both the current entry point and the original revision; if both are missing, leave it unknown rather than filling the gap with an adjacent fixture.

**Is a failing sample a regression item or an unstable signal?**

Classify into tiers first, then attribute the cause. A sample that can be reproduced consistently can be included in the regression tier; a sample seen only once, or missing its revision and raw results, should initially stay on the unstable-signal side. This classification lets maintainers continue investigating; it is not a determination of the cause. ATXA-001 documents a missing window in the middle of the Q&A; the missing section should be left blank.

**What goes into the handoff?**

Provide the entry point, the sample's location, and the revision, including whether it has been confirmed or is still missing. Content that still belongs to spec · Quality Signal Board stays on this page and in its attachments; if the issue has gone beyond the spec or fixture, hand over only the reproduction entry point to the maintainers of the relevant interface, without transferring this project's schedule along with it. If a failed run needs on-call attention, you can pick up from the on-call log at DOC-27, but don't treat that unfinished record as this page's conclusion.

versions.body:
# Caller Migration Guide: Old and New Entry Points

To migrate a caller, first find its entry in `docs/adj-httparty/migration/current-entrypoint-legacy-entrypoint-migration-index.md`. The index is populated from actual call samples; a new name appearing in the directory does not mean the caller has switched. Samples for `example` and `adapter` should be reviewed separately: the former shows what the user actually passes in, while the latter shows where the adaptation boundary lies. When both point to the same caller, use the entry point that caller is currently using.

## Recording Entries

Keep four columns for each migration item: old entry point, current entry point, caller, and rollback notes. Do not overwrite the old entry point with the new link; if the same name appears under different revisions, split it into two rows. Keep notes that cannot be traced back to a specific caller in the index and mark them as outdated. Do not infer from them that migration is complete.

`reproduction trace` is suitable for recording the call sequence leading up to a failure, while `last URI` records the last point reached separately. Do not combine the two into one field: the index already contains cases where they lead to different failure exits. When investigating a migration failure, fill in these two records first, then determine whether the entry point replacement is incomplete or `adapter` is still using the old adaptation method.

## Switching Order

1. Identify the corresponding `example` or `adapter` for the actual consumer, and record the old entry point it is using.
2. Add the current entry point to the same row and retain the original call sample; do not just change the display text.
3. Verify that the new entry point works with that caller. Determine whether migration is complete based on confirmation from the actual consumer, not on whether the index already lists a current entry point.
4. If the call passes through an adaptation layer, verify the caller's input and the adaptation layer's output separately. A successful result from the adaptation layer cannot substitute for the input held by the caller.

The callers currently using `multipart boundary` have not yet been fully recorded, so records involving this item can only be marked as pending confirmation; do not classify them based on other samples. `content encoding` and `host boundary` should also be kept as notes on their respective calls; they are not a basis for grouping multiple callers into a single migration batch.

## Reverting to the Old Entry Point

If validation of the new entry point fails, restore the old entry point originally recorded for that caller, while keeping the current entry point column and the failure record. Do not delete the old-to-new mapping as part of the rollback, or next time it will be impossible to distinguish between no migration, migration followed by rollback, and both entry points coexisting. After restoring the old entry point, recheck only the affected caller; continue handling other entries based on their own samples.

The index is continually updated with call samples from httparty-client-integration. For new records, clearly identify the caller and entry point first, then add the adaptation boundary. Do not merge entries whose names are merely similar but do not share the same call sample.
