versions.body:
# Postmortem on Two Versions of the Caller Record

This was initially left as a narrowly scoped field record: there were two revisions at the same entry point, and both labels said current revision. Only on later review did it become clear that the issue was not whether a record was still there, but that people reading the entry point could not tell which assessment corresponded to the caller in front of them. The last URI in the old record already differed from the value seen later, yet both versions of the content still appeared side by side with the same "current" status.

The entry point had not gone missing, and the records had not been overwritten, so the situation did not initially look like a failure. What was actually affected was the comparison process: someone saw one conclusion in an earlier revision, then retrieved a later revision from the same entry point, with no version boundary separating the two conclusions. Continuing to retry requests in this state could at best produce new results, but could not establish which record should no longer be used as the current entry point.

The initial response was to preserve the original input and the entry point version at the time, then stop further retries. This stopping point was deliberately conservative: the fact that multipart boundary could be restored did not mean the change in content encoding had also been explained. The early records did not combine the two issues into a single cause, nor did they therefore mark the scope of adoption as confirmed.

## How the Records Gradually Became Readable

| Stage | Recorded facts | Conclusions not reached at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | Two revisions shared the current entry point; last URI differed from the old record | Which revision the caller should adopt |
| After preserving the incident state | multipart boundary could be restored | The reason for the change in content encoding |
| After document review | The entry point file and the actual execution location needed to be checked separately | The file's existence was enough to show that the current result was executable |
| During review of the exit action | It must be possible to withdraw the old relationship and confirm that it is gone | Migration was complete across the full scope of adoption |

This table does not treat each check as a separate incident. It only records how understanding changed: the URI difference was noticed first, and only later were "the entry point is still there" and "the current result actually has an execution line" separated into two distinct matters.

The document review at the start of the year brought the issue back to the entry point's structure. ATXB-002 first recorded that the documents had been reviewed, then moved into formal review; this shows that someone had already started working on the content on an existing branch at the time, but it does not prove that the two revisions had been merged. It established a concrete place for the review work, not a root-cause conclusion.

ATXB-005 was later marked as failed, and work to address it began. Here, "failed" should be understood to mean that the current entry point was insufficient to support the caller's assessment, not as an assertion that httparty-client-integration was unusable as a whole. The distinction matters: a sample call can work normally while the entry point record still mixes the old and new revisions.

A field note added later made the gap more specific: the exit entry point file was still present, but the current result had no execution line. This observation overturned the early interpretation that "being able to open the entry point means the exit action is complete". The entry point file only shows that there is somewhere to enter; the execution line shows whether the current result is actually connected at that location. When the execution line is missing, the file path should not be used to infer that the withdrawal has taken effect.

The second addendum split verification into two boxes: one for whether the file exists, and another for whether the execution line exists. At that point, the exit entry point had only passed the first check. This split did not require rewriting all historical records in a uniform format, but simply avoided conflating the visible file, the current revision, and the execution location that could actually be reached at the same entry point.

The constraints used for comparison were narrowed accordingly. The requirement left in ATXB-007 was to hold httparty-client-integration, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and replace only the current revision. This was not intended to create a new release validation, but to avoid being unable to tell where the URI difference came from after changing the input, entry point, and revision at the same time. The card calls for a single-variable rerun; it is not presented here as a run result that has already been obtained.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Same entry point] --> B[Two revisions]
    B --> C{Can the current labels distinguish them}
    C -- No --> D[Save the original input and entry point version]
    D --> E[Check the file and execution line separately]
    E --> F{Do both checks for the exit entry point pass}
    F -- No --> G[Retain the incomplete assessment]
    F -- Yes --> H[Then check whether the old relationship is gone]
```

The "pass" in the diagram is not a generalized acceptance status. It only describes the two locations that need to be confirmed in sequence in this record: first confirm the entry point file, then the execution line for the current result. If the latter is missing, there is not enough of a basis to continue comparing revisions; if both are present, it is still necessary to check separately whether the old relationship has been withdrawn.

The recovery assessment therefore remains two-layered. The first layer is the partial recovery already observed: multipart boundary can be restored. The second layer remains unresolved: why content encoding changed, whether the change occurred only in this pair of revisions, and the extent to which the old record was actually used. The early page was right to leave these questions blank; the later material also provided no evidence sufficient to fill in those blanks with a cause.

Reproduction by someone other than the author was placed in ATXB-010, with a requirement to reproduce this case of "the two versions of the record not being merged" according to the release and run checklists, stopping if any item was missing. It is suitable for checking whether someone else can understand the records through the same entry point, not for replacing the historical assessment on this page. In particular, when the execution line is missing, even if the person reproducing the issue finds the file, they should record the missing item as an incomplete entry point rather than choose one of the revisions themselves.

ATXB-015 retains another, narrower check: replay the exit action corresponding to this incident to confirm whether the old edge really disappears. This action addresses withdrawal of the old relationship, which is not the same as recovery of multipart boundary. While the old edge remains, information from both revisions can continue to be returned through the same entry point; disappearance of the old edge also cannot, by itself, explain the change in content encoding.

# Compatibility Window Freeze Decision Record

This memo preserves the trade-offs made at the time of the compatibility-window freeze. When the discussion began, the existing request-policy entry point was already in use, but several claims around it had only intermediate processing values to point to. One proposal was to adjust the compatibility window first: make the window look closer to the paths the implementation could reach at the time, then add caller samples later. The other view was that the entry point could stay, but the window could not endorse compatibility behavior that had not yet been reproduced.

The latter approach was chosen. The existing entry point was left unchanged, and the freeze recognized only what the available material covered; "adjusting the window" was not treated as a way to make up for missing evidence. This decision left edge paths unspecified: readers could not infer all historical behavior from the window's name. The meeting accepted that gap between the name and what readers could establish, because turning those blanks into scope commitments would make them harder to retract later.

An early draft contained a stronger working judgment: seeing the same value during request processing was enough to show that the caller had not lost it. That sentence was later struck out, but its original intent should remain here. It reflected the urgency at the time to connect internal paths with external compatibility, not a confirmed fact.

After review, the role of the temporary value was reconsidered. It could show only that a particular step had obtained the value; it could not show what was retained when the request entered the entry point, or what the caller actually received after the response was returned. The value might appear before parsing, after serialization, or in an error branch. It could still help narrow the search, but could not support a compatibility window judgment on its own.

The original sentence left from the meeting was: "Keep caller input bytes beside the parsed or serialized result." It was later expanded into a more complete order for making the judgment: Start from a reproducible request, the raw response or emitted body, and the caller-visible object; an internal temporary value is not accepted as compatibility evidence. This did not require collecting every form of output every time. On the request side, compare the emitted body with the input; on the response side, compare the raw response with the processed result. Whichever side is being examined, do not stop at an internal variable: the caller-visible object must still be visible.

This distinction addressed the dispute over that freeze, rather than defining general layers for the request implementation. The bytes the caller handed to the request layer and the object visible after processing had to be included in the same sample to show whether a change occurred during parsing, serialization, or handoff. With only an internal value, the most that could be offered was a guess; it did not establish where the input came from or where the result ultimately went.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Existing request-policy entry point"] --> B["Reproducible request"]
  B --> C["raw response or emitted body"]
  C --> D["caller-visible object"]
  D --> E["Scope recognized by the freeze"]
  A --> F["Adjust compatibility window"]
  F --> G["Not adopted"]
```

There were two direct reasons for rejecting the window adjustment proposal. First, downstream users would read the window as the supported scope; changing it without caller samples would mean making an external judgment first, then looking for material to prove it. Second, internal temporary values could not establish the relationship between caller input bytes and visible results. The meeting did not deny the debugging value of those values; it only refused to elevate them to a basis for release.

At the time, a trace-back was done via `lib/httparty/request.rb` and related call names. That location grounded the discussion in request, bytes, raw, response, body, and temporary value, but it was not the permanent home of those objects. The old record had described "visible in the code" in terms very close to "external compatibility has been confirmed"; this addendum narrows that inference, not the entry point itself.

The readability issue raised by those who originally supported adjusting the window remained: the entry point name and the reproducible scope did not always line up at a glance. Expanding the window did not resolve that issue. Another unconfirmed point also remained: when the same request produced both a parsed result and a serialized result, the freeze did not decide whether both should be included in the sample. It only ruled out using screenshots or snippets of temporary values in place of caller material.

DOC-44 retains the switchover handoff for downstream SDK reproduction and can serve as a starting point when adding samples later. It does not change the trade-off already made here. If new caller reproductions become available, the input bytes, the raw response or emitted body for that path, and the caller object should still be compared; whether to open a separate window adjustment discussion should be considered only once that material is complete.

This page's old conclusion can therefore be read only as the freeze decision made at the time: retaining the request-policy entry point did not mean that every nearby path had entered the compatibility window.

# Multipart Memory Discrepancy Postmortem

This record preserves an incident-time assessment that is now outdated but is still often brought up: when the multipart memory profile window showed a discrepancy, the most conspicuous thing was the profile itself, so it was initially easy to treat it as an error in the profile itself. The later review did not produce a single root cause that could replace all the old explanations. It only narrowed that view: the discrepancy in the window can no longer be explained in isolation from the request state and redirect transition trace.

The original plan was to look at the results from the same window together. After the discrepancy appeared, the observed results did not line up with the original plan. Here, "did not line up" retains its original narrow meaning: it does not mean that all multipart requests failed, nor that an existing stable memory curve was disproven; it only means that the results from this window could no longer be compared using the original grouping method. The first action taken on site was to narrow the window, so that continued observation would no longer mix this data with later samples.

This action was later abbreviated as "recovery," which easily caused misunderstandings. What it restored was the conditions for continued observation, not the source of the anomaly, and even less a conclusion about the multipart path. After the window became usable again, the old trace, the lookup entry point from that time, and the unanswered questions all remained. The postmortem is long because these remnants are closer to the actual state at the time than the four-character phrase "recovery succeeded."

## Assessment Retained from the Initial Record

The initial draft compressed the phenomenon into two sentences: the profile window was off; first, shrink the window back. This wording was sufficient during the shift because it explained why the comparison results from that window could not continue to be used; it also had an obvious gap: later readers would misread "shrink the window back" as "the profile had already been fixed."

The working hypothesis in the initial draft was as follows, with its original intent preserved: the discrepancy might have come from the sampling or comparison method of the multipart memory profile; address the profile side first, then see whether any other signals remained. This was a convenient starting point, not an attribution that had already been proven. Its reasonable aspect was that the anomaly first appeared in the form of a profile-window discrepancy; its limitation was in the same place—it did not explain why the redirect transition trace left at the scene needed to remain under review.

The trace was not treated as the primary object at the time, not because it was irrelevant, but because the window first had to be contained. First contain a window that could no longer be compared, then bring out and review the request flow: that was the actual order of operations for that work. If the order is reversed and written as "complete the state analysis first, then restore the window," it actually makes the incident look more orderly than it was.

The initial draft also recorded `lib/httparty/cookie_hash.rb` as a lookup entry point. This information should be retained, but it should not be expanded into a judgment about module ownership. The investigation began by following the cookie call name and file location, with the goal of cross-checking the state retained during the request against the redirect transition trace. It shows where the investigation initially anchored; it does not mean that this file permanently owns all multipart or redirect issues.

## Changes Over Time Within the Window

**Discovery.** When a window from the multipart memory profile was used for comparison with the original setup, the results diverged. The divergence was first a matter of comparability: results that had been expected to be considered together could no longer be directly considered together. At this point, there was not enough evidence to classify it as memory growth, boundary handling, or a request format error. All that was known at the time was that continuing to add more results to the same window would make subsequent assessments harder to disentangle.

**Narrowing.** The action taken was to narrow the window. The immediate effect was to stop expanding the comparison scope that had already become distorted. No conclusion was recorded here that "the values returned to some fixed state after narrowing"; all that was established was that the window stopped taking in new results. This distinction became important later: an anomalous window that has stopped expanding is not the same thing as an anomalous window that has been fully explained.

**Temporary recovery.** After the window was narrowed, work could proceed, so this was described at the time as a temporary recovery. The material from after recovery was not cleared, and the redirect transition trace in particular was retained. The trace was not retained to provide an after-the-fact justification for the action taken at the time, but because it crossed the boundary of the earlier focus on the profile alone: if the request state changed the assumptions underlying the observations during the redirect transition, looking only at the window's final form could not explain when the deviation began to matter.

**Initial investigation.** The investigation started with the cookie call name and carried out a limited look-back along `lib/httparty/cookie_hash.rb`. In the old records, this path looked like "finding the cookie file," but it was actually narrower than that: it only allowed the people involved at the time to ask whether the cookie state still existed while the request was being redirected, and whether that state could appear alongside other headers. No results were recorded that were sufficient to identify this path as the root cause.

**Review.** The later review changed the investigation priorities. The profile was still where the anomaly appeared, but it was no longer treated as the only explanation. The review shifted the focus to the state changes corresponding to the redirect transition trace and required header coexistence to be examined in the same check. This did not mean that all the problems were caused by redirect; it acknowledged that the earlier single-point explanation did not account for the material retained from the incident.

This timeline deliberately does not add specific times. What the original records support is the relative sequence: discovery first, then narrowing, continued investigation after temporary recovery, and then a review of the old assumptions. Adding seemingly precise minute counts to each step would only manufacture another set of nonexistent incident evidence.

## What was actually affected at the time

The first thing this anomaly affected was a comparison window. The samples in the window should no longer have been used as part of the original setup, because the deviation had already made them incomparable. This impact is enough to explain why narrowing was prioritized at the time, without having to describe the entire multipart capability as unavailable.

The second layer of impact was the increased cost of assessment. The shape of the profile could easily draw attention toward memory, while the redirect transition trace pulled the investigation back toward request state. These two pieces of material were not mutually exclusive evidence: the former showed where the deviation was observed, while the latter was a reminder that the deviation could not be explained solely by that location. Failing to place the two side by side at the outset allowed the term "window problem" to be used too broadly.

The third level of impact was that the risk of header regression had not been closed out. The initial draft had already mentioned the case where cookie and authorization appeared together, but at that point it was only a branch pending review. The checkpoint added later was not intended to declare that this branch had been fully verified, but to avoid ending the investigation prematurely after seeing only a single header. After the window was restored, this risk remained in the record, indicating that the recovery action had not replaced the header checks.

There is no material supporting an expansion of the impact to all redirects, all cookie handling, or all multipart requests. This postmortem keeps the scope narrow, not to downplay the incident, but because what was observed at the time was a specific window and a trace segment. Rather than presenting an unverified scope as the impact, it is better to have subsequent investigations start from the known intersection.

## Why the initial assessment went in the wrong direction

"The profile shows a deviation, so the profile is at fault" is a very natural working hypothesis. It allowed the team on the scene to address an obvious operational problem immediately: stop contaminating the same comparison window. It also omitted a key premise—the profile only presents the request process that has already occurred; it does not necessarily determine that process.

The initial assessment was not completely invalidated by what followed. The window did show a deviation, and narrowing it was indeed a necessary temporary action. What was overturned was the treatment of these two facts as a sufficient causal link: just because the anomaly was visible in the memory profile did not mean that the memory side had already supplied the cause.

The redirect transition trace was the source of the counterexample. It was not interpreted in the record as a complete root-cause chain, but it was enough to undermine the premise that "looking only at the profile is enough." When a request redirects, the reader must ask two smaller questions at the same time: whether the cookie state is still present, and whether authorization coexists with it. Answering only one of them still leaves header regression outside the window.

This revision of the assessment is more accurate than "finding the real cause." What the review produced was an adjustment to the investigation boundaries, not an alternative, all-purpose attribution. The record contains no evidence showing which specific header, which state change, or which segment of multipart handling ultimately produced the deviation. Keeping the unknowns here prevents those who reference the record later from treating the old window as an implementation issue that has already been closed.

## What the temporary recovery left behind

After the window was narrowed, the most important things left behind were not a "recovered" marker, but three types of material: window results that could no longer be included in the original comparison, the redirect transition trace, and traces of searches near the cookie entry point. Each served a different purpose.

The window results explain why the team stopped adding to that interval at the time. They can no longer be interpreted under the original arrangement, but they still show that the deviation was discovered during the comparison process, rather than guessed at in an abstract discussion. Subsequent reviews should neither repackage these results as stable samples nor ignore the fact that they had invalidated the grouping.

The trace indicates that the request process is still worth revisiting. It was retained even after the temporary recovery, precisely because the recovery did not answer how state carried across the redirect transition. The value of the trace is not that it lets anyone derive a definitive implementation conclusion directly from it, but that it provides a concrete record from the incident to revisit when examining the header coexistence issue.

The cookie call name and `lib/httparty/cookie_hash.rb` record the starting point of the investigation. This point was very brief in the old notes and could easily be misread as "cookie_hash is where the problem lies". It was actually retained because, at the time, the retained state of the cookie was considered worth examining alongside the headers after the redirect. The file path was where the investigation landed at the time, not a prescribed order for future troubleshooting.

Together, these three types of material explain the limits of the temporary recovery: the window could be scaled back first, but the investigation could not be reset to zero as a result. Any summary that records only "recovery complete" would miss this boundary and hide the header issue that still needed to be reviewed later.

## Rereading the redirect transition trace

Before the review, the trace was treated as material that existed alongside the window. After the review, it became material that limited the earlier attribution. No complete request model was added between these two readings; the change was simply an acknowledgment that the trace meant the investigation could not stop at the surface of the profile.

In this incident, the significance of the redirect transition was not as a separate incident category. It was the point at which to check whether state persisted across request stages. The cookie was the object investigated from that starting point, while authorization was the object that had to be examined together with the cookie in the header regression branch. Recasting either one as a "confirmed failing header" would go beyond what the record can support.

The incident record did not contain a complete request sequence from which all the details could be reproduced, nor did it contain results sufficient to compare every header combination. Therefore, the role of the trace in this postmortem is to mark the boundary of the evidence, not to provide an answer. It shows that the earlier account, which closed out the issue solely on the basis of the profile, was insufficient; it does not show that a more specific state change had been pinned down.

When people later look at this material, they often ask why the trace contents were not written directly into the conclusion. The reason is straightforward: what needed to be preserved at the time was the fact that "the redirect was still within the scope of the investigation", not an unconfirmed explanation filled in for the trace. The postmortem therefore places it within the changes over time and the revised account after review, rather than turning it into a complete protocol walkthrough.

## Control point for header regression

The original wording of the control point added after the review is as follows:

> Do not close a header regression until cookie and authorization coexist.

It was included in this postmortem not as a general header rule, but because the window discrepancy in this incident had already exposed the limitations of looking at the profile alone. When cookie and authorization are not included in the same check, the investigation may end prematurely after an apparently acceptable state is observed; the redirect transition trace is precisely what makes that premature ending no longer reassuring.

This statement also must not be read in reverse as "as long as both coexist, the anomaly will definitely occur." The record provides no such causal relationship. What it requires is the minimum review condition before closing the header regression: both must appear in the same observation before it is possible to determine whether this branch has truly been ruled out. The focus here is the closure condition, not a prediction condition.

The checkpoint was added after the temporary recovery. This sequence shows that a complete assessment was not yet available at the time of recovery. Writing the checkpoint into the initial on-site decision would project later caution back onto that decision; simply deleting the initial draft's profile assumption would make it impossible to see why the review needed to change direction. The coexistence of these two accounts is what makes this record worth retaining.

The checkpoint did not replace the original handling of the window either. When a window discrepancy appears, the first step is still to stop expanding the interval that cannot be compared; the header coexistence check addresses whether the subsequent investigation can end, not how to make that window usable again immediately. Combining the two into one step would once again confuse "temporary recovery" with "investigation closure."

## Old Note on the Starting Point for the Cookie Search

The old note only stated that a search had been carried out using the cookie call names and `lib/httparty/cookie_hash.rb`. During the second editing pass, it was not expanded into a file-level conclusion, because this investigation focused on how request state was understood during the redirect transition, rather than redefining responsibility for a particular source file.

This starting point still has practical value. When faced with a similar window discrepancy, readers can see that the assessment at the time was not simply a guess based on the profile graph: the starting point for the cookie search had been cross-checked against the trace. It moved the investigation from "memory looks abnormal" to "is the request state complete?"

But this starting point cannot support anything more. It does not explain every change to cookie, nor where authorization is generated, much less all the call relationships involved in multipart processing. Adding those details would make the postmortem appear complete, but would obscure the gaps genuinely left by the original material. The path is retained here so that the old search clue remains recognizable, not to elevate it into an architectural explanation.

## An Outdated Paragraph That Was Not Deleted

> First confirm whether the memory profile has recovered; if it has, the window issue can be closed for now, and the remaining trace recorded separately.

The paragraph above is the most potentially misleading part of the initial draft. It is retained here to explain why the checkpoint was added later. It puts "profile recovery" and "window issue closure" in the same sentence, assuming that the trace can be handled separately from this anomaly. After review, that assumption no longer applies.

The existing records cannot support treating profile restoration as a closure condition. Being able to continue observing after the window narrows only shows that the temporary action was effective; the redirect transition trace and the header co-existence branch are still outstanding from the same review cycle. The old paragraph was not quietly changed into the new wording, because doing so would make readers think that cookie, authorization, and the redirect process had already been considered together from the beginning.

Another outdated shorthand is "the cookie path has been checked." In early communication, it was used to mean that the lookup had started, but it could later be understood as meaning that the cookie branch had been ruled out. The more accurate meaning in the old context is: cookie call names and related files were revisited as entry points, and the check did not automatically produce a closure conclusion. This qualification should be retained in subsequent references.

## Questions still not answered by this review

First, whether the deviation is limited to this multipart memory profile window. The existing material shows that this window cannot continue to be compared according to the original plan, but there is not enough scope to determine whether the same pattern will occur in other windows. Calling it a general multipart problem would expand a local anomaly into an unobserved scope.

Second, which part of the state change in the redirect transition is related to the deviation. The trace was retained and used to rule out a single-point attribution, but this record did not complete a segment-by-segment explanation. It can only show that the redirect process cannot be ruled out; it cannot show that any particular redirect step has been confirmed as incorrect.

Third, what the co-existence check for cookie and authorization would rule out. The control point specified the conditions that must be seen before closing the header regression, but it did not predetermine the result. The record lacks a result from a round that could directly link this condition to the window deviation, so it cannot be written up as a completed validation.

Fourth, how new samples after the temporary restoration should be separated from the old window. What is known is that they cannot be mixed back into the original comparison; what is unknown is whether there is a continuous boundary sufficient to restore the old comparison. This issue was not resolved at the time, nor did it disappear when the control point was added.

Fifth, whether the cookie lookup entry point still needs to be extended to other request states. `lib/httparty/cookie_hash.rb` was a local point of focus at the time, and cannot be used to infer that the remaining paths have already been covered. If this entry point is searched again in the future, first confirm whether the issue being handled is the same type of window deviation or a new problem that is only similar in name.

These unanswered questions are not a substitute for a to-do list. They separately show what the retrospective can provide: a window that lost comparability, a temporary restoration, a trace that changed the troubleshooting direction, and a condition that prevents the header regression from being closed prematurely. Causal relationships beyond these should still not be fabricated from this old record.

## Operational relationships

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[multipart memory profile window bias] --> B[Narrow the window]
  B --> C[Temporary recovery]
  A --> D[Retain redirect transition trace]
  D --> E[Cookie lookup entry]
  E --> F[Review cookie and authorization coexistence]
  F --> G[Do not close header regression early]
```

In the diagram, the path from window bias to temporary recovery indicates the order of on-site handling; it does not mean that profile has been identified as the root cause. The trace leading to the cookie lookup entry indicates how the review moves away from the initial single-point assumption; likewise, it does not mean that the file location assigns responsibility. The final path expresses only a control point: header regression cannot be closed until cookie and authorization have been observed together.

## Wording for subsequent references

This material continues to be cited because it preserves a very specific change in position: it was initially handled as a profile window issue, and then the conclusion that "window recovery is enough to close it" was withdrawn because the redirect transition trace remained. When citing it, include both facts—the temporary recovery and the undetermined root cause; citing only either one would flatten the incident.

If only the on-call procedure for parser fallback is needed, DOC-47 has a separate cheat sheet; it is not a continuation of this review, nor does it add any multipart attribution that was not recorded here. The focus here remains the window bias, state review, and the header regression that was not closed early.

Finally, retain one easily overlooked conclusion: this review raised the closure standard, not the certainty of the attribution. The profile window bias did occur, narrowing the window once allowed on-site work to continue, and the coexistence of cookie and authorization later became a necessary control point; as for the specific mechanism that ultimately connects them, this record does not reach a definitive conclusion.

# Parser fallback on-call procedure

When a parser fallback audit message comes in, first save the authentication version, the unprocessed results, and the multipart byte sample, and record the public entry point that triggered it.

1. Obtain the smallest reproducing request or payload and write down the observed transition.
2. After finding the corresponding module owner, hand off the first point of divergence, noting the local artifact that owner can inspect; route evidence from adjacent projects to the corresponding owner.
3. Stop if access needs to be expanded or public behavior changed; that is outside the on-call decision scope.

# Compatibility Window Result Discrepancy Troubleshooting Tree

The freeze is marked complete, but the review result can't be recovered. First write down the diagnostics entry point and version; stop if either is missing. Once both are present, compare the marshal round-trip transcript for the same input.

- Match: the ticket is missing the diagnostic source.
- Mismatch: record it as a header regression first; don't determine the cause in this meeting.

Still open: Can cookie and authorization appear at the same time? Who retains the original output?

# Compatibility Window Result Discrepancy Troubleshooting Tree

The freeze ticket is marked complete, but there was no reproducible result when it went to review. Don't send the ticket back yet; first record the diagnostics call entry point, version, and whether the marshal record came from the same input.

```text
Result cannot be reviewed
├─ Are the diagnostics call entry point and version documented?
│  ├─ No: stop here; ask whoever submitted the result to add the entry point and version
│  └─ Yes: take the same input and continue
└─ Compare the marshal round-trip transcript
   ├─ Match: the freeze record is missing the diagnostic source; add it back to the ticket
   └─ Mismatch: record it as a header regression and stop
```

This review did not merge the two outputs into one result; record the difference on a separate line. For a header regression, only check whether cookie and authorization can both be retained. Leave this line with the meeting: `Do not close a header regression until cookie and authorization coexist.`

If another diagnostics record is still needed here, or the explanation needs to be handed to a new owner, stop the tree here. Don't use the number of consecutive reruns to vote between the two results.
